solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

indicatorNotes.wrapping around: the purple word is wrapped around the abbreviation for 'around'

annotation.surface: Some purple packaging has been wrapped around a biscuit.
annotation.walkthrough: Maroon is a brownish crimson that crosswords happily call purple, and CA (circa, Latin for 'about') is the standard abbreviation for 'around'.
annotation.definitionFit: A macaroon is one kind of biscuit, made with almond or coconut, so the definition works by category.

annotation.surface: Dealing with the tax office is a burden.
annotation.walkthrough: HMRC (His Majesty's Revenue and Customs) is the UK tax authority.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses are one word: an onerous task is taxing (a plain synonym), and levying tax is literally what HMRC does all day.

indicatorNotes.in: the article is placed inside the newspaper's name

annotation.surface: Someone orders a drink after reading an article in a French paper.
annotation.walkthrough: "article in French" suggests LE or UN, but the article is English A, and "French newspaper" is Le Monde.
annotation.definitionFit: Lemonade is simply one kind of drink, so the definition works by category.

annotation.surface: A student is working with some splendid fabric.
annotation.walkthrough: L for learner comes from the L-plates on a learner driver's car.
annotation.definitionFit: Lace is a delicate open-work fabric, so 'material' defines it by category.

indicatorNotes.crossing: the friend spans the river, so ODER sits inside MATE

annotation.surface: A level-headed companion crosses the river Oder.
annotation.walkthrough: The Oder is a river on the German-Polish border; the surface has a friend crossing it, the wordplay has MATE straddling it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: measured and avoiding extremes, as in a moderate proposal.

blocks.note: the admiral who won at Trafalgar, flagship HMS Victory
a wrestling grip applied under the opponent's arms

annotation.surface: A triumphant sailor is being kept in a ship's hold.
annotation.walkthrough: "Victorious" nods to the flagship Victory as well as to Trafalgar; "hold" wants to be part of a ship, but it is a wrestling hold.
annotation.definitionFit: The first sense is a definition by example (the Trafalgar admiral); the second is a wrestling hold, as in 'full ___'.

indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, 'up' reads the word from bottom to top

annotation.surface: A squirrel's nest sits a yard up a tree.
annotation.walkthrough: Drey is the usual spelling, but DRAY is a recognised variant.
annotation.definitionFit: A dray (usually spelt drey) is the specific word for a squirrel's nest.

entries.clue: Old woman harbouring a convict in resort (6)

indicatorNotes.harbouring: the old woman shelters the convict inside her

blocks.note: A + LAG, an old lag being a convict

annotation.surface: An elderly woman hides an escaped prisoner at a holiday resort.
annotation.walkthrough: LAG is British slang for a convict, usually an old lag.
annotation.definitionFit: Malaga, on Spain's Costa del Sol, is a resort by example.

entries.clue: Rotter unwell with a cold in luxury motor (8)

annotation.surface: A cad with a cold is being driven around in a big car.
annotation.walkthrough: "with" just strings the pieces together; a rotter is an old British word for a cad.
annotation.definitionFit: Cadillac is an American luxury car brand; 'motor' is British for car.

entries.clue: Airline left India for Indonesian island (4)

annotation.surface: An airline leaves India on its way to an Indonesian island.
annotation.walkthrough: "left India" reads like departing the country, but it is L then I.
annotation.definitionFit: Bali is the best-known island of Indonesia, defined by example.

entries.clue: King Henry beginning to open Greek letter (3)

indicatorNotes.beginning to: take only the first letter of 'open'

annotation.surface: King Henry starts to open a letter written in Greek.
annotation.walkthrough: "King Henry" is one monarch in the surface but two pieces here: R and H.
annotation.definitionFit: Rho, the Greek R, is one letter of that alphabet, defined by category.

entries.clue: Gaol rebuilt houses barbarian in Calvary (8)

indicatorNotes.rebuilt: the letters of GAOL are put together again in a new order
indicatorNotes.houses: the rearranged gaol takes the barbarian inside

annotation.surface: A rebuilt prison holds a barbarian at the site of the Crucifixion.
annotation.walkthrough: GAOL is the British spelling of jail.
annotation.definitionFit: Golgotha (Aramaic) and Calvary (Latin) are two names for the hill of the Crucifixion.

entries.clue: Emperor once in Beirut is replaced (8)

indicatorNotes.replaced: the letters are placed again in a new order

annotation.surface: A former emperor has been replaced in Beirut.
annotation.walkthrough: "in" is just a link; the fodder is "Beirut is".
annotation.definitionFit: The definition works by example: Tiberius was a Roman emperor, and 'once' marks him as historical.

annotation.walkthrough: "Cooler" looks like a comparative adjective, but it is slang for prison, as is NICK (British slang, also a police station).
annotation.definitionFit: 'The cooler' and 'the nick' are both slang for prison, and a nick is also a small notch or groove.

entries.clue: A bicycle crashed striving to avoid it (8)

indicatorNotes.crashed: a crashed bicycle is a jumble

annotation.surface: A cyclist crashed while trying to swerve round something.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is playful: "it" is a coy word for sex.
annotation.definitionFit: The definition is whimsical: celibacy means abstaining from sex, the coy 'it', so it is the practice of avoiding it.

indicatorNotes.bears: the name carries the answer within it

blocks.note: the letters sit in the middle of the pharaoh's name, after TUT

annotation.surface: Tutankhamun is pictured carrying a cross, with a question mark at the idea.
annotation.walkthrough: Fittingly, the pharaoh's name really contains the Egyptian symbol of life, which the question mark acknowledges.
annotation.definitionFit: An ankh is the looped cross of ancient Egypt, so 'Cross' defines it by category.

entries.clue: Crone is eating good Scots food (6)

indicatorNotes.eating: the crone-and-is pair takes the G inside

annotation.surface: An old woman is tucking into some Scottish fare.
annotation.walkthrough: The eater is the crone and "is" together, so the G lands between them rather than inside the crone alone.
annotation.definitionFit: Haggis, spiced offal cooked in a sheep's stomach, is Scotland's national dish, defined by example.

entries.clue: Social event hosting dancing here in boozer (4,4)

indicatorNotes.hosting: the ball has the jumbled letters inside it
indicatorNotes.dancing: the letters of HERE move about

annotation.surface: A party with dancing is being held at the local pub.
annotation.walkthrough: A boozer is British slang for a pub.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Boozer' is British slang for a pub, and a beer hall is a large pub, so this is a regional-slang synonym.

indicatorNotes.curtailed: cut off its tail, the last letter

annotation.surface: A school's hard-fought debate was cut short.
annotation.walkthrough: Harrow is a famous English public (private boarding) school in north-west London.
annotation.definitionFit: Harrow is a school by example, one of England's best-known.

entries.clue: Parrot magpie ignored every so often (3)

indicatorNotes.ignored every so often: letters of magpie are skipped at regular intervals, leaving the others

annotation.surface: A parrot is left out now and then in favour of a magpie.
annotation.walkthrough: "Parrot" and "magpie" both look like birds, but Parrot is a verb: to ape is to copy.
annotation.definitionFit: As verbs, to parrot and to ape are synonyms: both mean to copy mindlessly.

indicatorNotes.announced: spoken out, so the sound counts, not the spelling

annotation.surface: A sensible ticket price has been declared.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes "Reasonable" describe the price, but it stands alone as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as in a fair price or a fair request.

indicatorNotes.battered: something battered has been beaten out of its proper shape, so the name's letters end up disordered

annotation.surface: Cain, the first murderer, battered people.
annotation.walkthrough: Cain killed his brother Abel in Genesis; here he is just four letters.
annotation.definitionFit: The name of the Andean people of Peru, so 'People' defines by category.
annotation.definitionNote: People is plural; INCA can name the people collectively.

annotation.surface: Someone is polishing a mystery gem.
annotation.walkthrough: "Polish" is capitalised to look like the nationality, but it is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Stone' here means gemstone, and the red gem is one, a definition by example.

annotation.surface: A pack animal such as a mule has a sore tendon.
annotation.walkthrough: "pack animal" reads as one beast of burden, like a mule, but it splits into two separate pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A ganglion is a fluid cyst on a tendon sheath, so 'tendon problem' is a descriptive definition.

entries.clue: Pick clubs and hearts over diamonds (6)

annotation.surface: A card player chooses clubs and hearts rather than diamonds.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface treats all three as suits, but only two are: diamonds is ICE, and O comes from an over in cricket.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain noun synonyms, as in 'take your pick'.

entries.clue: Man’s setting off as he chases girl (5,3)

indicatorNotes.off: the letters of AS HE are set off in a new order
indicatorNotes.chases: to chase is to run behind, so the shuffled letters come after the girl's name

annotation.surface: A man sets off in pursuit of a girl.
annotation.walkthrough: "Man" is the Isle of Man; "setting off" looks like a phrase but splits into definition and indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man lies in this sea between Britain and Ireland, so 'Man's setting' defines it by where the island sits.
